title: Are You Becoming the Dad You Want to Be?
author: Gareth Wall
summary: Dad coach Gareth Wall asks fathers to redirect the attention they give to their children's behavior toward their own reactions, habits and inherited patterns. He argues that recurring flashpoints such as bedtime battles and shouting reveal something worth being curious about, including what fathers tell themselves a behavior means and what they absorbed in their own childhood homes. A key move is to stop judging oneself by intentions, because children experience only what actually happened, and to ask instead whether a response was helpful. Wall emphasizes modeling, repair after mistakes and focusing on what a father can actually control. The piece ends with a long list of self-examination questions and a pitch for his free course and coaching.
points: Wall shifts the question from why a child is misbehaving to what happens inside the father when the child does it.
Many parenting reactions are inherited habits from one's family of origin that were never consciously chosen.
Children experience what a parent actually did, not what the parent meant to do, so intentions are not a defense.
Repair after getting it wrong, including a real apology, teaches children that relationships can survive mistakes.
quotes: That is a much harder question to ask ourselves. It requires us to be vulnerable. It requires an admission of being imperfect that might clash with our identity.
Sometimes what we react to isn’t just our childs behaviour, it’s what we have been conditioned to think what the behaviour means.

Some things we deliberately keep because we think they were good and some things we deliberately reject as we didn’t like them or thought they could have been better. And some things we carry with us without ever really deciding whether we believe them, they become habits.
But your child doesn’t experience what you meant to do, they only experience what actually happened.
Sometimes we spend so much time focused on what everyone else needs to do differently that we stop looking at the one person we actually have some control over.
The question isn’t whether you ever mess up. The question is what happens afterwards.
People can get things wrong and repair them. You see the relationship as being much more important than looking weak.
